tldr: We introduce WB-WAM, a World Action Model combining video generation and physical whole-body action prediction. By learning a shared 72-dimensional action space across heterogeneous, partially annotated sources and using VR human demonstrations for mid-training, it enables advanced humanoid loco-manipulation with very little real-robot data.
hero_caption: Overall architecture and three-stage training framework of WB-WAM. The top illustrates the pipeline: pre-training, PICO mid-training, and real-robot adaptation. The bottom shows the video DiT and action DiT coordinating conditioned on vision, language, and proprioception to drive the humanoid G1 via the SONIC controller.
overview:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating leg locomotion, trunk balance, and delicate dexterous hand control all at once. However, conventional robot pre-training datasets focus mainly on single arms or wheeled bases, leaving whole-body humanoid motion severely underrepresented. Meanwhile, existing human sources are fragmented: egocentric human videos capture hands without full-body motion, while motion capture datasets capture body joint trajectories without paired video.

To tackle this, the authors developed WB-WAM, extending the World Action Model (WAM) framework—which jointly predicts future video and action trajectories—to whole-body control. The core idea is defining a shared 72-dimensional physical action space unifying the body, root, and dexterous hands. This allows joint learning from heterogeneous data with partial annotations using loss masking. In addition, they built a three-stage curriculum with a "PICO mid-training" phase using egocentric human demonstrations recorded with commercial VR headsets (PICO), efficiently transferring human motion skills to the robot.

In evaluations, WB-WAM set new state-of-the-art records across all 7 tasks in the simulated HumanoidArena benchmark with an 81.9% success rate. On a real Unitree G1 robot across five daily assistance tasks, it achieved an 84.0% mean success rate. Notably, task-aligned PICO mid-training allowed a 70% cut in real-robot demos (from 100 down to 30) while still beating direct training on the full demonstration set.
contributions: Proposing a humanoid World Action Model that integrates video generation with explicit whole-body and hand action supervision, enabling large-scale learning from heterogeneous, partially annotated data.
Defining a shared 72-dimensional physical action space combining 29 DoF for the body, 3 DoF for the root, and 40 DoF for both dexterous hands, unifying roughly 1,900 hours of video and motion data.
Establishing a three-stage training pipeline featuring mid-training on egocentric human demonstrations captured via VR headsets (PICO), drastically reducing the cost of real-robot teleoperation data.
Achieving state-of-the-art results on the HumanoidArena simulation benchmark and outperforming six existing baselines in real-world humanoid loco-manipulation.

sections.heading: Whole-Body Humanoid Challenges and WB-WAM's Approach
sections.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation guided by vision and language requires coordinated whole-body locomotion and dexterous manipulation. Because existing datasets focus on wheeled robots or single arms, WB-WAM scales up joint video and action pre-training on heterogeneous, partially labeled data.
sections.details:
For general-purpose humanoid robots to assist in homes and workplaces, they must seamlessly coordinate leg locomotion with delicate multi-finger manipulation based on camera feeds and language instructions. Recent large-scale robot pre-training has advanced rapidly, but mostly focuses on static arms or wheeled bases. This leaves data coverage of humanoid-specific whole-body coordination severely lacking.

Meanwhile, World Action Models (WAMs)—which simultaneously learn to predict future video and generate actions—are gaining traction. However, utilizing internet data and human videos runs into severe data fragmentation: egocentric videos capture hand manipulations without whole-body walking data, while whole-body motion capture datasets lack camera footage.

To address this challenge, the authors introduce WB-WAM. Built on Fast-WAM, it defines a 72-dimensional physical action space unifying the body, root (pelvis pose/velocity changes), and dexterous hands. Using loss masking for missing annotations, it pre-trains video dynamics and whole-body actions simultaneously on 1,880.2 hours of video and motion data. Furthermore, introducing a mid-training stage using egocentric human demonstrations captured with PICO VR headsets allows the robot to achieve high task performance with minimal real-robot demonstrations.

sections.heading: The Landscape of Humanoid Foundation Models and World Action Models
sections.summary: Existing humanoid foundation models often operate on latent representations or task-space actions, rarely predicting interpretable joint references directly during pre-training. Conventional WAMs also focus predominantly on upper-body manipulation. WB-WAM stands out by directly coupling physically meaningful whole-body and dexterous hand trajectories with video generation.
sections.details:
### II-A Loco-Manipulation Foundation Models for Humanoids
Recently, foundation models learning visuomotor robot priors from heterogeneous data (such as GR00T N1, $\Psi_0$, WholeBodyVLA, and OpenHLM) have emerged. However, these models typically extract latent discrete actions from video or learn task-space actions that are later converted to joint commands using robot data. Directly predicting dense, physically interpretable whole-body joint trajectories suitable for controller inputs right from large-scale video pre-training remained largely unexplored.

### II-B World Action Models (WAM)
WAMs couple the internal dynamics of video world models predicting future frames with robot action generation. Yet most existing WAM research targets fixed-base arms or upper-body manipulation on wheeled robots. Even when applied to humanoid motions, they often rely on simplified motion plans or latent variables for controllers. In contrast, WB-WAM explicitly defines a physical space unifying body, root, and dexterous hand channels, directly incorporating large-scale whole-body action supervision right into generative video pre-training.

sections.heading: Mastering Whole-Body Control with a 72D Action Space and a 3-Stage Curriculum
sections.summary: WB-WAM uses a Mixture-of-Transformers with video and action experts to manage a 72-dimensional whole-body action space. It refines the model across three stages—heterogeneous pre-training, PICO mid-training, and real-robot adaptation with forward kinematics loss—and skips future video generation at inference for fast execution.
sections.details:
### III-A Preliminaries: World Action Modeling via MoT
WB-WAM builds on the multi-modal Flow Matching framework of Fast-WAM. The architecture employs a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) containing a video expert and an action expert, where the action expert attends to video expert features via MoT attention. Future frames are represented in the latent space of a pre-trained VAE, while the action expert predicts normalized physical motion trajectories.

### III-B Problem Formulation and the 72D Physical Action Space
The model receives an egocentric RGB image $\mathbf{I}_t$, robot proprioception (joint positions, etc.) $\mathbf{s}_t$, and a language instruction $\ell$. The target action $\mathbf{A}_t$ is a 72-dimensional vector comprising:
- $\mathbf{q}_t^B \in \mathbb{R}^{29}$: Whole-body joint position references for the Unitree G1
- $\mathbf{r}_t = (\phi_t, \theta_t, \omega_t^z) \in \mathbb{R}^3$: Root roll, pitch, and yaw angular velocity
- $\mathbf{q}_t^L, \mathbf{q}_t^R \in \mathbb{R}^{20}$: Joint references for the left and right Wuji dexterous hands

### III-C Stage I: Heterogeneous Body-Hand Pre-training
Training leverages roughly 1,900 hours of data spanning video+body+hand, video+hand, and text+body motion. Since annotations vary across sources, a binary mask $\mathbf{M}$ is applied so flow velocity loss is computed only on present channels (Eq. 4). To reduce computational overhead during deployment, the action tokens randomly attend to either the entire video sequence or only the current single frame during training. This lets the policy bypass future video generation (IDM) at runtime, predicting actions directly from the current image.

### III-D Stage II: PICO Motion Mid-training
The pre-trained model is mid-trained on egocentric human demonstrations collected via VR headsets (retargeted to body, root, and hands). This instills task-aligned physical contact and kinematic priors before touching the real robot.

### III-E Stage III: Robot Task Adaptation
Finally, the model is adapted on real-robot demonstrations for each task. Here, an auxiliary differentiable forward kinematics (FK) loss (Eq. 6) penalizes skeletal pose discrepancy between reconstructed and ground-truth joint positions, ensuring structural consistency. During deployment, the predicted body and root trajectories feed into the whole-body controller SONIC for locomotion and balance, while hand trajectories are executed as direct joint commands.

sections.heading: Curating 1,900 Hours of Pre-training Data, VR Headset Demos, and Robot Teleoperation
sections.summary: Alongside 1,880.2 hours of pre-training data compiled from nine external sources, the authors collected 22 hours of egocentric human demos via PICO and 1,011 real-robot teleoperation episodes via SONIC, supported by a rigorous quality-filtering pipeline.
sections.details:
### IV-A Heterogeneous Pre-training Data (1,880.2 Hours)
In Stage I, nine external datasets were integrated, including Xperience-10M, EgoDex, and MotionMillion. Human motions were retargeted to the G1 morphology using General Motion Retargeting (GMR), and hand motions were mapped to the Wuji hand joint space. Rigorous filtering with automated detectors and manual checks eliminated unnatural poses, discontinuous joint trajectories, self-collisions, and corrupted video frames (such as blank or frozen frames).

### IV-B Egocentric PICO Mid-training Data
Operators wore PICO 4 Ultra headsets and five trackers on their hands, feet, and waist to record 20 Hz egocentric RGB video and full-body motion. Whole-body inverse kinematics (IK) enforced joint limits and avoided self-collisions, while hand poses were estimated from video using MINT and retargeted to Wuji hands. This yielded 73 tasks and 13,396 episodes (totaling 22 hours).

### IV-C Real-Robot SONIC Teleoperation Data
Real-robot data were gathered using the SONIC whole-body teleoperation system across eight tasks: table wiping, curtain closing, bed making, pillow relocating, cart pushing, checkout, clothes organizing, and fruit pick-and-place. This dataset comprises 1,011 episodes (3.37 hours, 242,668 frames).

sections.heading: Simulation and Real-Robot Tests Validate Whole-Body Coordination and Data Efficiency
sections.summary: WB-WAM achieved an 81.9% average success rate in the HumanoidArena simulator, beating all existing baselines across every task, and reached 84.0% across five real-robot tasks. Furthermore, PICO mid-training enabled a 70% reduction in real-robot demonstrations while maintaining higher success rates.
sections.details:
### V-A & V-B Implementation and Deployment Setup
The backbone uses Wan2.2, with the action expert being a smaller DiT initialized via structural parameter transfer. On the physical Unitree G1 equipped with an Intel RealSense D455, WB-WAM runs at roughly 0.7 Hz, predicting 32-step action chunks. The robot executes 20 of these steps at 20 Hz, routing body and root targets through SONIC (50 Hz tracking, 500 Hz motor commands) and hand targets directly as joint commands.

### V-D 1 Simulation Evaluations (HumanoidArena)
Evaluated on seven whole-body loco-manipulation tasks involving object interaction and environmental contact, WB-WAM achieved an average success rate of 81.9%, outperforming the strongest reported baselines across all seven tasks.

### V-D 2 Real-Robot Comparisons
On the physical G1, WB-WAM was compared against six baselines: ACT, $\pi_{0.5}$, GR00T N1.6, Fast-WAM, DiT4DiT, and OpenWAM across five tasks (three loco-manipulation and two stationary whole-body tasks, 20 trials each). WB-WAM achieved an 84.0% mean success rate, surpassing the strongest baseline, OpenWAM (80.0%). The performance gap was especially pronounced on mobile tasks (76.7% vs. 71.7%). Baselines frequently failed due to approach positioning drift, missed grasps, and desynchronization between walking and arm motions.

### V-E Demonstration Reduction via PICO Mid-training
The impact of mid-training versus demo quantity was evaluated. Directly training on 100 real-robot demos resulted in a 65.0% success rate. In contrast, the model with PICO mid-training achieved a 73.8% success rate with only 30 real-robot demos (a 70% reduction). Compared to direct adaptation on the same 30 demos (48.8%), mid-training delivered a massive boost, proving that human VR demonstrations effectively compensate for scarce robot data.

### V-F & V-G Language Following and Visual Generalization
Qualitative evaluations confirmed that a single policy accurately picks between apples, lemons, and oranges based on language commands. It also demonstrated visual robustness by steadily pushing a cart under novel visual conditions where unexpected luggage altered its appearance.

sections.heading: Wrapping Up and Looking Ahead
sections.summary: WB-WAM establishes a World Action Model capable of learning whole-body physical actions from incomplete, heterogeneous datasets. By leveraging VR-based human demonstrations, it offers a practical path to drastically reduce real-robot data requirements. Future work aims for zero-shot transfer to novel tasks and finer contact control.
sections.details:
This study introduced WB-WAM, a World Action Model incorporating explicit whole-body, root, and dexterous hand action supervision into generative video pre-training. Through a shared 72D physical action space and loss masking, it effectively harnesses 1,880 hours of disparate heterogeneous data.

Furthermore, mid-training with egocentric human demonstrations captured via VR headsets substantially reduced the need for real-robot demonstrations while enhancing downstream performance. This provides a highly practical blueprint for humanoid robotics, where collecting real-world data is notoriously expensive.

As future challenges, the authors note that current evaluations were restricted to a single platform (Unitree G1) and required per-task adaptation. Key future directions include improving zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks and refining fine-grained control during physical contact.

takeaways: When coupling video and action models, defining a shared physical action space (body, root, hands) with loss masking allows a single model to absorb heterogeneous, partially labeled data (video-only, motion-only, hand-only).
Mid-training on egocentric human demonstrations recorded with VR headsets (PICO) and body trackers cuts costly real-robot teleoperation data by 70% while outperforming direct training.

Stochastically switching between full-sequence video attention and single-frame attention during training allows the model to bypass future video generation (IDM) at runtime, enabling low-latency action generation.
limitations: Experiments are limited to a single robot morphology (Unitree G1), leaving cross-embodiment transfer to other humanoids or different DoF setups unverified.
Real-robot deployment fine-tunes a separate policy (weights) per task, falling short of a fully unified multi-task policy or zero-shot execution on unseen tasks.

The retargeted human mid-training motions only provide kinematic references; dynamic balance and contact force guarantees on the physical robot still rely on the downstream SONIC controller and robot-specific adaptation.
